Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

new paragraph before the gym closed for the day the staff returned the counted equipment to the assigned storage areas and left the held items in their marked places the empty bins were stacked by the east entrance and the blue cart stayed beside the gym door for the driver the return sheet showed the twenty four tablets the twenty four counted charging blocks the two band cases and the three sealed science kits as returned it listed the cracked block the slide tray the auditorium stand and the unlocated mouthpiece folder as still awaiting their stated checks or location details ms ellis placed the sheet in the office tray and told nina that the team would review the remaining entries on monday if the technology aide had not checked the cracked block by then it would remain pending and would not be added to the completed charger count", "output": "At Cedar Ridge Middle School, the spring equipment return began on Thursday morning in the old gym because the main office hallway was being painted. The return involved instruments, science kits, sports gear, and two carts of library tablets that had been borrowed for the sixth grade project week. Ms. Ellis was coordinating the return with Mr. Chen from facilities and Nina Patel, the student council treasurer. The equipment had come from three storage rooms and several classrooms, so the staff wanted one shared record before anything was moved back to its usual shelf. The gym doors stayed open, but the west side entrance remained locked during delivery.

The first cart arrived at eight twenty with twenty-four tablets in padded sleeves and a small box of charging blocks. The inventory sheet listed twenty-six sleeves, but two had been set aside in the library for a repair check. The office had emailed that detail on Wednesday, although the printed sheet did not include it. Ms. Ellis said, “Please keep the two repair sleeves separate from the returning equipment and write their location on the blue tag.” Mr. Chen placed the blue tag beside the box rather than attaching it to either sleeve because the sleeves were still in the library. He asked Nina to confirm the charger count before the cart went through the gym doors.

Nina counted twenty-four charging blocks and found one block with a cracked corner. She did not say that it was unsafe; she said it was already marked for review in the library notes and should not be included in the returned charger count until the technology aide checked it. The class teacher had written that the tablets were all present but had not counted the blocks. Ms. Ellis compared the cart list with the email and entered twenty-four blocks as present and one as pending review. The cart remained beside the eastern wall while Nina looked for the aide. The return could continue if the pending item stayed clearly separate and was not mixed into the closed box.

The return checklist had three numbered entries:
1. Count each item against the room sheet and record any difference.
2. Attach a location tag to equipment that is being held for review.
3. Move only the counted equipment to its assigned storage area.

The list applied to all departments and not only to the tablet cart. Mr. Chen read each entry aloud because the gym was noisy with chairs being stacked nearby. Ms. Ellis asked that the storage room number be written on each tag, and Nina agreed to use the labels from the supply cabinet. The checklist did not give permission to discard or repair anything, and the staff had no plan to do either.

At nine ten, the band teacher brought two instrument cases, a stand, and a folder of mouthpiece covers. She asked if the cases could be returned before the full orchestra set because her next class began in the music room at ten. The cases were on the return sheet, but the stand was listed as belonging to the auditorium, and the folder had no room number on its cover. Ms. Ellis said, “Return the two cases with the band equipment and leave the stand and the folder on this table until we can check their labels.” The teacher agreed and pointed out that the stand had a yellow sticker from the auditorium shelf. The sticker gave a location but no staff name, so Mr. Chen left it visible for a later check.

The science teacher arrived with three sealed kit boxes and one open tray of glass slides. The boxes matched the list, but the tray had a handwritten note that said, “Inspect before storage.” The teacher explained that the class had used the tray for a demonstration and had returned every slide to its slot. She asked whether the tray could go on the science room cart while the note was being checked. Ms. Ellis said the tray could stay in the gym until the lab aide confirmed the note because the condition on the return sheet required any item marked “Inspect before storage” to remain outside the science room. The teacher took the three sealed boxes to the assigned cart and left the tray on a padded table with the note facing upward.

By ten thirty, the gym had separate areas for counted equipment, pending checks, and items with an unclear location tag. The tablets and charging blocks that had been counted were placed on the technology cart. The cracked block was in a small envelope marked “Pending review.” The two repair sleeves remained in the library, and the blue tag named the library as their location. The band cases were placed on the music cart while the stand and mouthpiece folder stayed on the table. The sealed science kits were on the lab cart, and the slide tray remained on the padded table. No one moved an item from one area to another without telling Ms. Ellis and writing the reason on the shared sheet.

The school secretary called at eleven to ask if everything had been returned because a delivery van was scheduled to collect empty storage bins after lunch. Nina said the return was still in progress and gave the secretary the count from the sheet. She did not report the pending items as missing and did not say that the return was complete. Ms. Ellis explained that the van could collect the empty bins if the staff kept the three holding areas clear. The secretary replied, “I can send the driver to the east entrance after lunch, but please leave the blue cart beside the gym door so nobody mistakes it for the empty-bin stack.” Mr. Chen marked the cart position on the floor plan and asked the caretaker not to shift it before the driver arrived.

At noon, the lab aide checked the slide tray and confirmed that all slides were in their slots, but asked to keep the tray in the lab until the science teacher could initial the sheet. The cracked charging block had not yet been checked because the technology aide was helping a student with a login problem. The auditorium clerk confirmed that the yellow sticker on the stand meant the auditorium shelf but could not confirm whether the music department had borrowed it with permission. The mouthpiece folder still had no room number. Ms. Ellis recorded these updates without closing the relevant entries. The condition for moving the slide tray remained the teacher initial, and the pending charger remained outside the counted total until the aide reviewed it.

Before the gym closed for the day, the staff returned the counted equipment to the assigned storage areas and left the held items in their marked places. The empty bins were stacked by the east entrance, and the blue cart stayed beside the gym door for the driver. The return sheet showed the twenty-four tablets, the twenty-four counted charging blocks, the two band cases, and the three sealed science kits as returned. It listed the cracked block, the slide tray, the auditorium stand, and the unlocated mouthpiece folder as still awaiting their stated checks or location details. Ms. Ellis placed the sheet in the office tray and told Nina that the team would review the remaining entries on Monday. If the technology aide had not checked the cracked block by then, it would remain pending and would not be added to the completed charger count."}]
